claims.text: Protective oxide development and retention are primarily governed by the preferential oxidation and diffusion kinetics of a key reactive element such as Cr or Al.
High configurational entropy ensures a uniform distribution of the reactive element.
At high temperature, the reactive element rapidly forms Cr2O3 or Al2O3.
A continuous and adherent Cr2O3 or Al2O3 scale limits further oxidation.
The baseline alloy contains a moderate concentration of Cr or Al homogeneously distributed in the matrix.
Increasing the concentration of the reactive element enhances its oxidation tendency.
Increasing the reactive-element concentration enhances its diffusion toward the surface during high-temperature exposure.
Enhanced surface-directed diffusion preferentially produces a continuous and adherent protective oxide layer.
The high-entropy nature of the alloy minimizes local compositional inhomogeneities.
Reduced local compositional inhomogeneity favors uniform oxide-scale growth.
The alloy with increased reactive-element content will form a thicker oxide layer than the baseline alloy.
The alloy with increased reactive-element content will form a more continuous and adherent oxide layer than the baseline alloy.
The alloy with increased reactive-element content will show lower weight gain than the baseline alloy.
The alloy with increased reactive-element content will show lower oxide-scale defect density than the baseline alloy.
The baseline alloy will form a less uniform oxide scale than the modified alloy.
The baseline alloy will form a thinner oxide scale than the modified alloy.
The baseline alloy will have a higher oxidation rate than the modified alloy.
The proposed mechanism applies at approximately 1000 degrees Celsius in an oxidizing atmosphere.
The proposed mechanism may not apply at lower temperatures or in reducing atmospheres because oxidation kinetics and diffusion behavior differ.
Failure of increased reactive-element content to produce a statistically significant oxidation reduction relative to the baseline would falsify the hypothesis.

contradictions.description: The prediction treats a thicker oxide scale in the modified alloy as an expected protective outcome, and the baseline is explicitly predicted to have a thinner scale. However, the falsification rule lists similar or higher oxide thickness in the modified alloy as evidence against the hypothesis. Thus, higher thickness is simultaneously a predicted result and a potential falsifier.
